verdict.note: The answer covers the resolver and dispatch logic accurately, but it omits the WorkbenchKeybindingService listener registration, the layout-aware keyboard mapper, how the resolver is built from the registry and user keybindings, and command activation in CommandService.

The answer covers the ext-host-side transport selection, the Ready/Init/Initialized handshake and ExtensionHostMain's RPCProtocol, but it never explains RPCProtocol's proxy, request and reply mechanics, the MainContext/ExtHostContext contract, the fact that the renderer (not the Electron main process) is the RPC peer, or the utility-process/MessageChannelMain setup, and it blurs 'renderer/main process' instead of stating that.

The answer wrongly puts the local extension host on a socket/PersistentProtocol path and places the drop points in PersistentProtocol.send and _receiveMessage, when the local host actually uses fire-and-forget MessagePort postMessage; it also says pending replies hang forever instead of being rejected as canceled by RPCProtocol.dispose, and it never covers the exit handling, disposal, restart, or Terminate behavior.

The answer covers the essential dispatch path (context lookup, resolver first-chord map, prefix filtering, newest-first when-clause scan, MoreChordsNeeded/KbFound/NoMatchingKb handling, executeCommand) and the IME guard, but it omits the workbench listener registration, the layout-aware keyboard mapper, lazy resolver construction in _getResolver with weight ordering and rebuilds, and onCommand activation in CommandService; it also leaves out the 5 s chord timeout and the 'not a command' message.

The answer covers the utility-process and MessagePort transport and the handshake well. It omits how RPCProtocol works internally (Proxy to _remoteCall, Acknowledged/Reply messages), the renderer-side MainThread* customer registration in ExtensionHostManager, the wire format and the other transports, and it wrongly says actors are obtained via getProxy(ExtHostContext.*) rather than registered with set.

The answer correctly covers the Shape declaration and MainContext entry, the main-side @extHostNamedCustomer class, the getProxy call site, Dto serialization and the unchanged wire layer, but it never states that the stub is generated only for names starting with '$'. It also omits the import from extensionHost.contribution.ts, the assertRegistered startup failure, the ExtHostContext callback registration and the vscode.d.ts API exposure.

The answer correctly covers the RPCProtocol request/ack/reply flow, the Ready/Initialized/Terminate handshake, and ExtensionHostMain's RPCProtocol/IExtHostRpcService setup. It says the renderer is the peer but omits the _createExtensionHostCustomers registration, extHost.protocol.ts shapes, utility-process/MessageChannelMain setup, wire format and other transports, and wrongly names ipc.electron.ts as a transport for this channel.

The answer correctly covers the fire-and-forget postMessage, the rejection of pending replies in RPCProtocol.dispose, and the PersistentProtocol contrast, but it misses the exit-event and crash-handling chain, the post-dispose dropping in _remoteCall and _receiveOneMessage, the 3 s unresponsive signal, the lost Terminate message, and the restart behavior; it also wrongly treats the MessagePort transport as the sole drop point and says renderer recovery is limited to dispose, which ignores the RPCProtocol-level dropping and the automatic restart.

The answer wrongly says the local desktop path is a PersistentProtocol, and its main drop point (the socket writer buffer and drain/flush) does not apply; it also cites ipc.electron.ts Protocol.send and BufferedEmitter.flushBuffer, which are not part of this path. It names the `_isDisposed` guard in `RPCProtocol._receiveOneMessage`, which is only part of q2f4, but leaves out the rest: the exit handling, the disposal that cancels pending replies, the Terminate loss, and the restart without replay.

The answer applies PersistentProtocol's ack/replay queue to the local crash path and calls an un-acked _outgoingUnackMsg entry the drop point, which conflicts with the fire-and-forget MessagePort send; it misses the RPCProtocol.dispose cancellation, the post-dispose drops, the exit handling, the lost Terminate message and the no-replay restart, and wrongly says the crashed host's grace timers fire onTerminate.

The answer explains the utility-process/MessagePort setup and the Ready/Init/Initialized handshake accurately, and correctly says the renderer is the RPC peer, but it omits _createExtensionHostCustomers. It only names RPCProtocol without describing the proxy/request/reply mechanics, the MainContext/ExtHostContext contract, or the extension-host-side actor registration, and it covers alternative transports only partially.

The answer correctly covers the shape/MainContext declaration, the @extHostNamedCustomer main-side class with the contribution import, the getProxy call site, serializable Dto types and the generic wire layer. It never explains why the $ prefix is required, omits that a missing customer makes assertRegistered throw at startup, and leaves out the vscode.d.ts API exposure.

The answer correctly covers the fire-and-forget postMessage, how the exit event reaches _onExtHostProcessExit, dispose rejecting pending replies, and the PersistentProtocol contrast, but it misses the essential crash-handling chain (_onExtensionHostCrashed/stopAllInReverse/ExtensionHostManager.dispose), the post-dispose dropping in _remoteCall/_receiveOneMessage, the lost Terminate message, the unresponsive signal and the restart without replay; it also brings in BufferedEmitter, which plays no part in the reference path.

The answer explains the utility-process/MessagePort setup, the Ready/Init/Terminate handshake and ExtensionHostMain's RPCProtocol well, but it omits the RPCProtocol proxy and reply mechanics, the extHost.protocol.ts shapes and identifiers, the renderer-side ExtensionHostManager customer registration, the wire message format and the other host transports.

The answer covers the _doDispatch-to-KeybindingResolver.resolve core and IME bail-out well, but it omits the WorkbenchKeybindingService listener registration and the keyboard mapper details, gives only partial chord-mode handling (no status messages, 5s timeout, or NoMatchingKb branch), and omits how the resolver is built from defaults plus user keybindings and how CommandService activates extensions; it also names StandaloneKeybindingService._getResolver, which is outside the workbench path.
